notes.body_html: Yoma 86b: “R’ Yochanan said: Great is teshuvah, for it overrides a negative commandment of the Torah, as it says, ‘Saying: if a man sends away his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man’s, shall he return to her again? Would not that land be utterly defiled? Yet you have played the harlot with many companions; and return to Me, says Hashem’ (Yirmeyah 3:1)” — though a remarried divorcée is forbidden to return to her first husband, God says “return to Me.” R’ Tzadok: teshuvah avails even where the Torah’s own law would bar it. Maharal, Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah ch. 2 (§13 in Sefaria's segmentation), comments on these two statements of R' Yochanan together: "גדולה תשובה שמגעת עד כסא הכבוד" and "גדולה תשובה שדוחה את לא תעשה שבתורה." Their juxtaposition is conceptually exact. The Torah's prohibition marks the order appropriate to a world in which a broken marital bond cannot simply be restored after a second union. Teshuvah, however, reaches the Kisei HaKavod — the source above the ordinary created order — and therefore the prophetic "ושובו אלי" can disclose a relationship whose possibility cannot be generated by the legal structure alone. This does not mean halachah is suspended for human beings; the divorced wife remains prohibited by Torah law. Rather, the mashal teaches the transcendent nature of the Divine reception of teshuvah: Hashem can restore the sinner to a closeness that the finite legal analogy would declare irrecoverable.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 103a: “Menasheh did teshuvah, and ‘and He received his entreaty [va-yeichaser lo]’ (Divrei HaYamim II 33:13) — this teaches that the Holy One made for him a kind of tunnel [machteres] in the firmament, to receive him in teshuvah, [past] the Attribute of Justice.” Pesachim 119a: “‘the hands of a man beneath their wings’ (Yechezkel 1:8) — it is written yado [His hand], the hand of the Holy One spread beneath the wings of the chayos, to receive penitents from the hand of the Attribute of Justice.” Chagigah 15a: after Acher sinned, a bas kol announced “‘Return, wayward children’ — except for Acher”; hearing this, he despaired of being received, and gave himself over to sin. R’ Tzadok: Acher failed to grasp that the “hand” receives even against the strict law. The Ishbitzer's reading of Menasheh gives a remarkable inner background to the "machteres." Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Prophets, II Kings 21:1, says Menasheh was born with an overwhelming yirah that human strength could scarcely bear. His sin, in the Izhbitzer's formulation, began from seeking ways to remove that overpowering awe "בכדי שיהיה בעל בחירה" — so that he would possess a felt field of choice — because the intensity of the yirah seemed to take choice away from him. Whether or not one translates every detail of this daring teaching into R' Tzadok's system, its relevance is clear: Menasheh's corruption is not treated as proof that no holy root existed. The very point that became distorted had an original holy form. That makes the tunnel beneath the Kisei especially meaningful. Teshuvah does not merely negotiate with the externally visible record of Menasheh's reign; it reaches beneath it to the buried root from which even the distorted search for "bechirah" had emerged. The Middas HaDin, judging the acts in their revealed form, has no argument for such a return. The Holy One "digs" beneath that plane and receives the soul from its deeper source. This is a characteristically Ishbitz-Radzin way of understanding why even the architect of the churban can become a baal teshuvah: the shoresh and the revealed history are not identical.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §8): “The churban was through the sin of Menasheh, as is explicit in Scripture — yet it was not destroyed in his days, nor even at once in the generation after him, for the Holy One is ‘long of patience, though He collects what is His’; and though they are a later generation, the root of Knesses Yisrael is one in every generation.” This is the same middah by which §3-1 says teshuvah “is accepted even where, by strict law, it should not avail”: the very Menasheh through whom the House fell is met not by immediate justice but by God’s long patience — the attribute that holds justice back and makes room for return, reaching (as the se’if says) even to one for whom God “burrowed a tunnel beneath His Throne.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Sichas Malachei HaShareis §2): On the Yerushalmi (Makkos ch. 2) — “they asked the Torah… they asked the Holy One, and He said, ‘let him do teshuvah’” — R’ Tzadok explains: “by [the measure of] the Torah and chochmah, through the sin a blemish has been made in his soul, and with what shall that blemish be atoned? It requires something that atones. But by [the measure of] the Holy One — who alludes to the perfect Unity, the clear sensation that ‘Hashem is One’ and that He ‘fills the whole earth with His glory,’ with nothing else here at all — [teshuvah itself suffices].” This is exactly §3-1’s “overriding a prohibition of the Torah”: Torah and wisdom must reckon a residue that demands payment, but from the vantage of God’s own Oneness the sinner simply returns — teshuvah is the remedy above the Torah’s own accounting.

notes.body_html: Berachos 34b: R’ Abbahu taught, “in the place where baalei teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous do not stand,” deriving it from “peace, peace to the far and to the near” (Yeshayah 57:19) — peace is extended first to “the far one” (the penitent) and only afterward to “the near one” (the ever-righteous). That is why the tzaddik gamur cannot "stand" there: it is not a higher rung on the tzaddik's unchanged ladder but a place generated by the movement of return itself.

notes.body_html: Kiddushin 18a (first chapter): R’ Chiya bar Avin said in the name of R’ Yochanan that a gentile inherits from his father by Torah law, “for it is written, ‘I have given Mount Se’ir to Esav as an inheritance’ (Devarim 2:5)”; the Gemara objects, “ve-dilma Yisrael meshumad shani? — but perhaps an apostate Jew is different,” i.e. Esav was no gentile at all but an apostate Jew, so his inheriting proves nothing about gentiles (the point is instead proven from the descendants of Lot). The very objection establishes that even Esav — the archetypal renegade — is classed not as a non-Jew but as a “Yisrael meshumad,” an apostate who nonetheless retains the name and status of Israel. This is the basis for the settled halachah, which R’ Tzadok invokes, that a Jewish apostate’s “betrothals are valid and his divorce is valid”; for as the Sages said (Sanhedrin 44a), “even though he has sinned, he is [still] Israel” — the name “Israel,” rooted in Yaakov, cannot be uprooted from a Jew by any sin.

notes.body_html: Yoma 86a: the four levels of atonement. “One who transgressed a positive commandment and repented — is forgiven at once. One who transgressed a prohibition and repented — teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones. One who [committed sins bearing] kareis or court-death and repented — teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend, and sufferings scour [memarkin]. But one who has chillul Hashem in his hand — teshuvah has no power to suspend, nor Yom Kippur to atone, nor sufferings to scour; rather, all of them suspend and death scours.” R’ Tzadok: by Torah-law teshuvah alone never fully exempts — that limitation belongs only to “this world.”

notes.body_html: Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1: עבר על מצות עשה ושב — אינו זז משם עד שמוחלין לו; עבר על מצות לא תעשה ושב — תשובה תולה, ויום הכפורים מכפר… עבר על כריתות ומיתות בית דין — תשובה ויום הכפורים תולין, ויסורין ממרקין The Baal HaTanya opens Iggeres HaTeshuvah with the very baraisa this se’if expounds, and supplies the reason the se’if presupposes: even where the punishment is pardoned, “the light remains absent” — which is precisely why teshuvah, from the side of this bounded world, cannot of itself restore what was. The opening of Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah, is especially useful for R' Tzadok's distinction between selichah and complete restoration. The Alter Rebbe first cites the four-fold baraisa of Yoma and then insists that the essential Torah mitzvah of teshuvah is the wholehearted abandonment of sin; the subsequent categories describe what is still required for full kapparah and cleansing of the blemish. Thus immediate forgiveness and the remaining need for Yom Kippur or yissurin are not contradictions. A person may already be a genuine baal teshuvah while the spiritual effect of the past has not yet been fully cleared. That structure parallels the architecture of Takanas HaShavin: the earliest rung makes the person "healed" from now on, while later rungs address the harder question of the former reality itself. The Chabad formulation and R' Tzadok's formulation are not identical, but both refuse to reduce teshuvah to a single undifferentiated event.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 21:6: “‘And now [ve-atah], lest he stretch out his hand [and take also of the tree of life]’ — R’ Abba bar Kahana said: this teaches that the Holy One opened for him an opening of teshuvah, [for] ‘and now [ve-atah]’ is always [an expression of] teshuvah; but he [Adam] said ‘pen [lest],’ and ‘pen’ is always a negation.” R’ Tzadok: God offered an opening, but Adam’s sin (the death-decree) was not fully undone — the “tree of life” was withheld. A striking Izhbitz parallel makes the phrase "tree of life" almost a definition of the higher teshuvah discussed here. Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Bereishis 6, on "ועץ החיים בתוך הגן," writes explicitly: "ועץ החיים הוא תשובה אמיתיות שמרפאות את הקודם" - the Tree of Life is true teshuvah that heals what came before. He then associates the river Peras with baalei teshuvah and explains that teshuvah "מגיע למקורו הראשון," reaches the person's first source. This is precisely the distinction of the present se'if: ordinary compromise heals from now on, whereas access to the Tree of Life would mean reaching back to the first source and curing the prior deficiency itself. R' Tzadok himself supplies an essential safeguard in Pri Tzaddik, Shelach §6. He explains that teshuvah can transform the Tree of Knowledge into "very good," so that even deliberate sins become merits; but the mekoshesh erred by imagining that this might make it desirable to spoil first and repent afterward. The higher reading of the past is available only *after* a real fall has occurred and a real teshuvah has transformed it. It can never be used prospectively to authorize what the Torah forbids. Thus the Izhbitz-Radzin language of healing the original source intensifies moral responsibility rather than weakening it.

notes.body_html: Rosh Hashanah 17b: expounding the doubled Divine Name of the Thirteen Attributes — “Hashem, Hashem” — the Gemara teaches, “I am He before a person sins, and I am He after a person sins and does teshuvah,” for God does not hold the earlier sins against him, being ever “merciful and gracious.” The same passage is the source that “great is teshuvah, for it tears up a person’s sentence [gzar din],” derived from “and he shall return and be healed” (Yeshayah 6:10) — “what is it that requires healing? — say, that is a [sealed] decree.” R’ Tzadok fastens on the wording “I am He after he sins and repents”: the penitent is restored to God exactly as before the sin, with no trace remaining — the full retroactive rectification of the past, the rung that (like the tree of life) awaits the future. Sod Yesharim, Shabbos Chol HaMoed Sukkos 33:1 (Izhbitz-Radzin), develops the doubled Name in a way that closely matches R' Tzadok's "exactly as before." After citing "ה' ה' - אני הוא קודם שיחטא אדם ואני הוא לאחר שיחטא האדם ויעשה תשובה," it explains that the latter Name means that after sin and teshuvah Hashem illuminates the person "ממקום היותר נעלה" - from a still higher place. It further says that there remains a hidden point of connection that is concealed even from the heavenly hosts, and that "יכול רק השי"ת לבדו להראות התיקון איך שמעולם לא נפסק מזה האדם החיבור אף בשעת החטא" - only Hashem Himself can reveal the rectification, namely how at the deepest level the bond was never severed even during the sin. This is not a denial of the sin on the revealed plane; the same teaching distinguishes what can be seen by the created order from what Hashem alone discloses after teshuvah. It therefore gives unusually exact content to R' Tzadok's use of "אני הוא לאחר שיחטא": the restored identity is not merely a new relationship built after the break. Teshuvah can uncover a deeper, hidden continuity of the covenantal bond that the sin never reached, and from that hidden point the revealed rupture can itself be healed.
notes.body_plain: Rosh Hashanah 17b: expounding the doubled Divine Name of the Thirteen Attributes — “ Hashem, Hashem ” — the Gemara teaches, “I am He before a person sins, and I am He after a person sins and does teshuvah,” for God does not hold the earlier sins against him, being ever “merciful and gracious.” The same passage is the source that “great is teshuvah, for it tears up a person’s sentence [ gzar din ],” derived from “and he shall return and be healed” (Yeshayah 6:10) — “what is it that requires healing? — say, that is a [sealed] decree.” R’ Tzadok fastens on the wording “I am He after he sins and repents”: the penitent is restored to God exactly as before the sin, with no trace remaining — the full retroactive rectification of the past, the rung that (like the tree of life) awaits the future. Sod Yesharim, Shabbos Chol HaMoed Sukkos 33:1 (Izhbitz-Radzin), develops the doubled Name in a way that closely matches R' Tzadok's "exactly as before." After citing "ה' ה' - אני הוא קודם שיחטא אדם ואני הוא לאחר שיחטא האדם ויעשה תשובה," it explains that the latter Name means that after sin and teshuvah Hashem illuminates the person "ממקום היותר נעלה" - from a still higher place. It further says that there remains a hidden point of connection that is concealed even from the heavenly hosts, and that "יכול רק השי"ת לבדו להראות התיקון איך שמעולם לא נפסק מזה האדם החיבור אף בשעת החטא" - only Hashem Himself can reveal the rectification, namely how at the deepest level the bond was never severed even during the sin. This is not a denial of the sin on the revealed plane; the same teaching distinguishes what can be seen by the created order from what Hashem alone discloses after teshuvah. It therefore gives unusually exact content to R' Tzadok's use of "אני הוא לאחר שיחטא": the restored identity is not merely a new relationship built after the break. Teshuvah can uncover a deeper, hidden continuity of the covenantal bond that the sin never reached, and from that hidden point the revealed rupture can itself be healed.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 28:13: at the ladder-dream — “וְהִנֵּה ה׳ נִצָּב עָלָיו וַיֹּאמַר, אֲנִי ה׳ אֱלֹקֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִיךָ וֵאלֹקֵי יִצְחָק” — “and behold, Hashem stood over him and said: I am Hashem, the God of Avraham your father and the God of Yitzchak” — Yaakov’s first prophecy (Rashi: “stood over him — to guard him”). notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §11): “It is the beginning of cleaving to that which is above the Torah, and then he acts ‘within the line of judgment [lifnim mishuras hadin],’ for he goes out of the bound and limit of the Torah — for ‘chassid’ is a term of ‘chesed,’ meaning boundless [self-]abandon, for chesed is expansion without end.” The se’if’s “great is teshuvah” that overrides the judgment of Torah and sages: it acts from the side of the Holy One Himself, above the Torah’s own bounds.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ דְּמִקֹּדֶם שָׁאֲלוּ לְחָכְמָה, לַתּוֹרָה, וְלִנְבוּאָה — אֵין זֶה שִׂיחָה בְּטֵלָה וְדֶרֶךְ מְלִיצָה, רַק כָּךְ הוּא הַשּׁוּרָה הָרְאוּיָה וְסֵדֶר הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת לִהְיוֹת נִשְׁאָל לָהֶם קֹדֶם; וַעֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ הַשְּׁאֵלָה להקב“ה, וְשֶׁיְּבֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת, עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא מָשִׁיחַ הַשּׁוֹאֵל זֶה מהקב”ה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״חַיִּים שָׁאַל [מִמְּךָ] נָתַתָּ לּוֹ״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסֻכָּה נב.]
notes.body_html: Tehillim 21:5: “חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ, נָתַתָּה לּוֹ, אֹרֶךְ יָמִים עוֹלָם וָעֶד” — “He asked life of You; You gave it him — length of days forever and ever.” The Sages (Sukkah 52a) apply the verse to the King Mashiach: he “asks life” of the Holy One and is granted eternal life, “length of days forever and ever.” R’ Tzadok makes this the culminating rung: only with Mashiach does the “asking” reach the Holy One Himself (after the epochs of asking Wisdom, Torah, and Prophecy), and only then is the promise “death shall be swallowed up forever” fulfilled — the utter, retroactive rectification that no earlier rung could attain.

notes.body_html: Avodah Zarah 9a: “The world exists six thousand years: two thousand of chaos [tohu], two thousand of Torah, two thousand the days of Mashiach. From when are the ‘two thousand of Torah’ counted? From ‘the souls they made in Charan’ (Bereishis 12:5)” — when Avraham began teaching Torah and bringing souls to faith. R’ Tzadok aligns the epochs with “asking Wisdom” (until Torah), “asking Prophecy” (from Sinai), and “asking the Holy One” (Mashiach).

notes.body_html: Taanis 27b: “Avraham said before the Holy One: Master of the Universe, perhaps Israel will sin before You and You will do to them as to the generation of the Flood? He said: No. He said: How shall I know I will inherit it? He said: Take Me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, and a three-year-old ram (Bereishis 15:9) [the covenant of the pieces]. He said: This is well while the Temple stands — when it does not stand, what will be of them? He said: I have already established for them the order of sacrifices; whenever they read them before Me I will regard it as if they offered them, and I forgive them all their sins.” R’ Tzadok: with Avraham begins atonement-through-korban (and he “chose the exiles” — the scouring sufferings — since teshuvah alone does not fully scour).

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Poked Akarim §2): “for the Torah is ‘from Heaven,’ [given] through the apprehension of prophecy — [and] all Israel merited, at the standing of Har Sinai, the apprehension of prophecy then, ‘and they heard Anochi and Lo Yihyeh from the mouth of the Almighty’; therefore it is ‘an inheritance for all the congregations of Yaakov,’ and all are destined to attain this in the future.” This is §3-8’s own historical claim: the supra-Torah rung of teshuvah “from the side of the Holy One Himself” belongs to the age of prophecy that opened at Sinai — where the whole desert generation heard God directly, so that “if they are not prophets, they are children of prophets” (Pesachim 66a) — an “inheritance” awaiting all Israel in the future.

notes.body_html: Shmuel II 14:14: the wise woman of Teko’a, pleading with David to bring back the banished Avshalom, says — “כִּי מוֹת נָמוּת וְכַמַּיִם הַנִּגָּרִים אַרְצָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא יֵאָסֵפוּ, וְלֹא יִשָּׂא אֱלֹקִים נֶפֶשׁ, וְחָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח” — “for we must surely die, and are like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered; yet God does not take away a soul, but devises means that the banished one not be cast out from Him.” Rashi: “‘God does not spare a man’ from death — therefore the king should devise means [machashavos] that his outcast not remain banished.” R’ Tzadok takes “lo yidach mimenu nidach” as God’s own assurance that no member of Yaakov’s seed is ever finally cast off: though in this world there are apostates and deniers among Israel, at the future ingathering it will be “clarified to the eye” that no seed of Yaakov is rejected at all. Two major Chassidic traditions make R' Tzadok's use of "לא ידח ממנו נדח" especially concrete. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 39 (39:20 in Sefaria), explains the assurance that even Torah learned shelo lishmah will ultimately rise: a Jew's end is certainly to do teshuvah, in this gilgul or another, "כי לא ידח ממנו נדח." The Alter Rebbe thus reads the verse not merely as a promise that God will not abandon the person, but as a promise that the person's own buried Torah and avodah will eventually return with him when he returns. Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beit Yaakov 23:11, gives the Izhbitz-Radzin side of the same promise. The believer trusts that Hashem "חושב מחשבות לבלתי ידח ממנו נדח" and that whatever passes over him can ultimately be shown to have been for his good. Even events that presently seem impossible to reconcile can, through a clarity Hashem later opens in the mind, become the very ground of consolation. This is not a claim that every present act is good in its revealed form. It is a statement about the final Divine "machashavos" that refuse to let a Jewish soul's history end in banishment. Cf. Resisei Layla §35: even the consciously "nidachim" - those who know they are Jews yet have been driven far from the knowledge of Hashem - are promised awakening by the great shofar, because "לא ידח ממנו נדח." This sharpens the se'if's future tense: the fact that the root cannot be finally expelled will only be fully "clarified to the eye" when the outcasts actually return.

Berachos 10a: Yeshayahu told the ailing Chizkiyahu, “‘set your house in order, for you shall die and not live’ (Melachim II 20:1) — you shall die in this world and not live in the World to Come,” because he had not engaged in procreation (foreseeing wicked offspring). Chizkiyahu answered, “Son of Amotz, finish your prophecy and go: thus I have received from the house of my father’s father — even if a sharp sword rests on a man’s neck, let him not withhold himself from mercy.” R’ Tzadok: this is the revelation that nothing — not even a prophetic decree — stands before the request for Heaven’s mercy. R' Tzadok returns to this very Chizkiyahu-Menasheh episode in Pri Tzaddik, Bo §9. Chizkiyahu saw that a "ben delo ma'ali" would issue from him, yet Yeshayahu answered "בהדי כבשי דרחמנא למה לך"; and R' Tzadok adds that when Hashem gives children, the hidden outcome is necessarily toward good - for from Menasheh came the chain of Mashiach ben David, and even regarding Menasheh himself the dorshei reshumos found a share in the World to Come. What Chizkiyahu saw prophetically was true, but it was not the whole truth of the future chain.

Likkutei Torah, Pinchas 3:22, places "כבשי דרחמנא" in a still broader Chassidic frame: the "secret of the world" is the hidden dimension of Torah and of the Divine will, drawing from a level described there as Atik, beyond what the revealed order can display. This helps define the limit R' Tzadok is drawing. Prophecy may reveal what a future child will do; it does not thereby give the prophet jurisdiction over why that soul must exist or what ultimate tikkun will emerge through generations. The command belongs to the revealed Torah; the hidden accounting belongs to Hashem.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 24:16: “מִכְּנַף הָאָרֶץ זְמִרֹת שָׁמַעְנוּ, צְבִי לַצַּדִּיק, וָאֹמַר רָזִי לִי רָזִי לִי אוֹי לִי” — “From the corner of the earth we have heard songs, ‘Glory to the righteous!’; but I said, ‘My secret is mine, my secret is mine, woe is me!’” Rashi: the prophet heard from behind the heavenly Curtain that in the future songs would rise “from the corner of the earth” — the raising-up of the righteous; “‘razi li’ — woe is me that two secrets have been revealed to me, the secret of retribution and the secret of salvation,” for the redemption is delayed until wave upon wave of oppressors has come. R’ Tzadok takes “razi li” as the mark that the highest rung of teshuvah — already revealed to Chizkiyahu, that “nothing stands before teshuvah” — is one of the kivshei d’Rachmana, “known to Him alone and to no creature.” The continuation in Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beit Yaakov 23:11, sheds light on Yeshayahu's "razi li." Faith in Hashem's hidden "machashavos" includes trust that a person can eventually be given a da'as in which what was formerly unbearable is understood and consoled - "הצרות ישובו נחמות." Until that da'as is opened, however, the secret remains secret. The believer does not manufacture an explanation for the hidden decree; he continues in emunah while leaving its resolution to Hashem. This is a useful Izhbitz-Radzin complement to R' Tzadok's distinction here between the revelation that teshuvah always remains possible and the still-concealed *order* by which that possibility works. Chizkiyahu could reveal the rule "do not despair of mercy"; neither he nor Yeshayahu thereby possessed the complete map of how Menasheh, destruction, exile, and the Davidic chain would be woven into redemption.

notes.body_html: Devarim 29:28: “הַנִּסְתָּרֹת לַה׳ אֱלֹקֵינוּ, וְהַנִּגְלֹת לָנוּ וּלְבָנֵינוּ עַד עוֹלָם, לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת כָּל דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת” — “The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever, to carry out all the words of this Torah.” In its plain sense the verse divides jurisdiction over sin: what is hidden is left to Heaven, and only the revealed is given to the human court to punish (Rashi notes the dots over “lanu u-le-vaneinu,” teaching that Israel was not held answerable for the hidden sins of individuals until it had crossed the Jordan and taken on mutual responsibility). R’ Tzadok reads “ha-nistaros la-Hashem” as the kivshei d’Rachmana — the hidden counsels known to God alone — from whose side the great rung of teshuvah operates, overriding the Torah’s revealed judgments with no true contradiction. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Nitzavim 3, reads "הנסתרות לה' אלקינו והנגלות לנו ולבנינו... לעשות" as a direct rule for the boundary between hidden causation and human bechirah. A person may be tempted to say that a corrupt impulse did not truly come from him but from the spiritual atmosphere into which he was placed. The Izhbitzer answers from this verse: "ישתדל האדם לבער הרע מקרבו ולבדוק עד מקום שידו מגעת בנגלות, והשי"ת יעזור לו בנסתרות" - the human task is to uproot evil as far as his hand reaches in the revealed realm; Hashem will deal with and help him in the hidden realm. This is one of the clearest guardrails for reading the present se'if and, more broadly, the Izhbitz-Radzin discussions of foreknowledge and choice. "Kivshei d'Rachmana" are real, but they are *not* the field on which a person decides what he is permitted to do. His avodah is "the revealed things... to do all the words of this Torah." Only Hashem can disclose afterward how the hidden dimension was woven through the story. Thus "razi li" protects, rather than dissolves, the boundary of halachic responsibility.

notes.body_html: Berachos 10a: the Gemara recounts that when Yeshayahu told the ailing Chizkiyahu “you shall die and not live” — because he had not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation — Chizkiyahu explained that he had foreseen through ruach hakodesh that unworthy children (Menasheh) would issue from him. Yeshayahu answered: “bahadei kivshei d’Rachmana lamah lach — why do you involve yourself with the secret counsels of the Merciful One? What you are commanded, you must do; and what is pleasing before the Holy One, let Him do.” R’ Tzadok builds his whole se’if on this: the very existence of a Menasheh is from the kivshei d’Rachmana, and therefore his teshuvah and rectification are likewise from that hidden secret — so that teshuvah’s “overriding” of the Torah’s judgments is no contradiction, but a matter reserved to God alone, to be revealed in the future. The Chassidic application of "בהדי כבשי דרחמנא למה לך" is especially important because it prevents a deterministic misreading of the entire discussion. The revealed command to Chizkiyahu was peru u'revu; his knowledge of a future Menasheh did not allow him to calculate his way out of that command. R' Tzadok states the principle in Tzidkas HaTzadik §78 with exceptional force: had Menasheh not been born, the entire holy chain culminating in Mashiach ben David would, God forbid, have been lost - even though Menasheh stood among those whom the revealed Mishnah lists as having no share in the World to Come. The hidden good of a future outcome is therefore not something a person can calculate in advance. This is fully consonant with the Mei HaShiloach on Nitzavim cited above: the hidden things belong to Hashem, while man's obligation is to work within the revealed Torah. The paradox is deliberate. Divine foreknowledge can contain a redemptive end that prophecy itself does not encompass, while human bechirah remains accountable precisely because the person is commanded to act only on the revealed word.

notes.body_html: Shabbos 89b: “‘Though your sins be like shanim [scarlet], they shall be white as snow’ (Yeshayah 1:18) — Rabbi Yitzchak said: [read ka-shanim] like the years [shanim] that are ordered and come from the six days of creation, [yet] ‘they shall be white as snow.’” R’ Tzadok: sins that are, in truth, “ordered from the six days of creation” (from the kivshei d’Rachmana) are, from the hidden side, no sin at all — hence utterly whitened. R' Tzadok's own Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi §4, gives a fuller explanation of this difficult derashah of "כשנים." On the human side, he says, a stain that has penetrated through and through cannot simply be washed away: "מצד האדם אי אפשר לטהר א"ע מהחטא." Therefore the promise "כשלג ילבינו" requires a purification from Hashem Himself, from the hidden supernal source. He then reads "כשנים הללו שסדורות ובאות מששת ימי בראשית" as pointing to that concealed root which will be revealed in the future. The whiteness is not produced by calling the red stain white; it is produced by a Divine purification that reaches deeper than the layer in which the stain took hold. Sefas Emes, Purim 29:3, expresses the same transformation tersely: "אם יהיו חטאיכם כשנים כשלג ילבינו" - the sins are turned into merits, and the Purim reversal is a foretaste of the future, when the entire structure raised by Haman becomes the cause of his own fall. This offers a concrete model for R' Tzadok's language: the past is whitened when the very sequence that embodied danger becomes, through teshuvah and Divine reversal, the instrument of redemption. Again, the transformation is retrospective; it does not render the original wrong permissible.
